1969 Ford Cobra Barn Find Has a Rare Performance Option We All Love
18 photos
Photo: eBay/gregwill16
The Cobra name first appeared on a car when Carroll Shelby debuted his Ford-powered roadster in 1962 . Six years later, Ford debuted a high-performance engine called the Cobra Jet. The name also resurfaced on a series of limited-edition Mustangs in the 1990s. But did you know that Ford also used it on a short-lived muscle car?
In 1968, Ford launched the Torino. It was a premium sub-series of the Fairlane. The following year, Ford expanded the lineup with two models, a two-door Sportsroof (fastback) and a two-door hardtop. These cars are known as Torino Cobras or even Fairlane Cobras. Ford, however, sold them as Cobras, without Torino or Fairlane badges.
But the Cobra was more than just a Torino with a sleeker roofline. It was actually a stripped-down muscle developed to compete with the Plymouth Road Runner. The latter debuted in 1968, selling over 44,000 units. And while the regular Torino came standard with an inline-six, the Cobra rolled off the assembly line with the 428-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Cobra Jet.
A carryover engine from 1968, when it debuted mid-model-year, the Cobra Jet came with 335 horsepower and 440 pound-feet (597 Nm) of torque. It was Ford's most potent mill except for the 429-cubic-inch Boss V8 (375 horsepower), which was only available in the Mustang for NASCAR homologation purposes.
Much like the Mustang, the Cobra also got the Super Cobra Jet option. Included in the Drag Pak bundle, the Super Cobra Jet added cast pistons, special connecting rods, an oil cooler, and the option to select a 4.30:1-ratio rear end. These features made the Cobra more suitable for drag racing.
But the Ford Cobra was never as popular as the Road Runner. While the Mopar moved over 80,000 units in 1969, Cobra sales barely exceeded 11,000 examples. And most of them are still sitting in junkyards and barns, waiting for a second chance. The Gulfstream Aqua example you see here is one of those cars.
The fastback emerged in Winchester, Kentucky, and it looks like it hasn't been touched in decades . It's dusty, the front clip is weathered, while the interior is a bit messy. It's also been partially dismantled, with the drivetrain removed. However, it appears to be a solid project car over all. And the good news is that the owner still has the numbers-matching drivetrain.
He's looking to get rid of the car, and he's also offering a donor body that will supply "some of the necessary sheetmetal." The seller also compiled a long list of the "mostly original" parts. The engine has been checked to be original, but it's not 100% complete.
The seller says he's willing to sell just the body or only certain components (hence the list in the ad), but I'd sure like to see this 1969 Cobra purchased as is and restored. And I'll give you a good reason for that too: the Ford is much rarer than the overall production number suggests.
The four-speed gearbox makes it one of only 3,910 units built, while the Gulfstream Aqua color narrows it down to just 230 examples. If we also factor in the 3.91 Traction-Lok rear axle and the front bench seat, we're probably looking at one of fewer than 100 units built like this. The seller wants $27,500 for the whole car, but he's accepting offers. What's your take on this sticker?
